text:
alex_k: ran a 6h canary comparing fixed-interval (3ms) vs dithered coalesce (2-8ms) + kernel-affinity toggles. putting raw numbers here for visibility.

maria: great, drop the summary first — p50/p95/p99 and token-cost?

alex_k: sure. high level: fixed-3ms had slightly lower p50 but p95 regressed ~6% and p99 spiked on microbursts. dithered reduced p99 spikes, improved overall throughput by ~4%, but we saw kernel-selection flipping more frequently which upped CPU context switches. token-cost delta: ~-1.2% for dithered.

sam: can you paste the profiler snippets? curious about where kernel churn shows up.

alex_k: attaching quick snippet from perf-bot output (stripped):

```
perf-bot: flame: runtime_main -> coalesce_wait -> select_kernel (prefer-fast-kernel) -> copy_kv_cache -> kernel_exec
notes: kernel switch rate ~1.8x under dithered, vs 1.1x fixed.
```

ravi: did you also capture KV hit/eviction stats? switching kernels often can evict hot KV slices.

alex_k: yes — KV hit-rate overall down 2.7% in dithered runs. eviction count increased on nodes serving long-tail sessions.

maria: interesting. so fewer token-cost, less p99, but worse KV locality and more kernel churn. tradeoffs. were the p95 regressions concentrated on a subset of models/seq lengths?

alex_k: p95 regressions on fixed interval were mostly for short seq (<64) where batching benefited. dithered smoothed microburst arrivals so short seq saw fewer tail spikes. long-seq (>=512) had no meaningful change.

sam: what about queue policies? did you try eager-coalesce vs hold-first?

alex_k: we ran two queue policies: hold-first (prioritize earliest req until budget) and greedy (fill to token_budget then flush). hold-first + dithered = lowest p99 but slightly higher mean latency for small requests. greedy + dithered = best throughput but worst KV thrash.

ravi: kernel-affinity flag names? I want to test prefer-fast-kernel=false to avoid kernel flips on ephemeral batches.

alex_k: flags we toggled:

```
continuous_batching:
  coalesce_delay_ms: 2-8 # dithered range
  fixed_delay_ms: 3    # baseline
  jitter_strategy: dithered | none
  queue_policy: hold-first | greedy
  token_budget_target: 256 | 512
kernel_selection:
  prefer_fast_kernel: true | false
  affinity_cooldown_ms: 150
```

maria: what token_budget_target did you use in the canary?

alex_k: main runs used 256 target. we also ran a 1h sweep at 512; that reduced kernel flips (batches longer -> more stable exec path) but increased p50 by ~7% for tiny requests. overall cost-neutral if you care throughput.

sam: any perf regressions vs last release? perf-bot should have flagged.

perf-bot: regression sniff: p95 up 4.1% on release/2026-03-10 -> canary-fixed-3ms; p99 up 12% under microburst events. No CI regressions on unit tests.

ravi: given KV hit drop, we should instrument KV priming: maybe prefetch top-10 keys for long-tail sessions before kernel switch. Also increase affinity_cooldown to 300ms for dithered to reduce flip rate.

maria: agree. plan: 1) run a small cluster with dithered 2-8ms + affinity_cooldown 300ms + hold-first + token_budget 256; 2) parallel A/B with dithered+512 token_budget; monitor p50/p95/p99, KV hit-rate, kernel-switch-rate, and cpu_ctx_switches.

sam: add histograms for inter-arrival and per-batch kernel type sequence so we can correlate flips to arrival patterns.

alex_k: will spin up canary and share dashboard. quick note: we should also add a fallback policy that pins to fallback-lazy-kernel when KV hit-rate drops >5% to avoid QoS regressions.

maria: ok please create a GH issue with the config and dashboards. tag me and @ravi. if A/B shows no KV or p99 regressions we can try a staged rollout. :thumbsup:

alex_k: created issue: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/issues/1428 — includes configs, perf-bot logs, and dashboards. will post results here in ~6h.

ravi: thanks. quick follow: if affinity_cooldown helps, we might be able to lower the dither upper bound to 6ms and recoup p50. food for the sweep.

maria: perfect. let's reconvene after canary.

alex_k: thanks all.
